questions.q: What is the difference between JavaScript and Node.js?
questions.explain: JavaScript is the language. In the browser, the browser is the runtime. On your computer and on servers, the runtime is Node.js.
options: They are two names for the same thing
JavaScript is the language; Node.js is the runtime that runs it on your computer and on servers
Node.js is the language; JavaScript is the program that runs it
JavaScript runs on servers; Node.js runs only in browsers

questions.q: Which Node.js version does ZudoJS need?
questions.explain: ZudoJS needs Node.js 24 or newer. Check with node --version: the result must start with v24 or higher.
options: The newest test version, not LTS

questions.q: On the Node.js download page, why should you pick the LTS version?
questions.explain: LTS stands for long-term support. It gets fixes for a long time, so it is the stable choice. It must also be version 24 or newer.
options: LTS means long-term support: the stable version most companies run
It is the only version that includes npm
It is the only version that works on Windows

questions.q: You installed Node.js, but your open terminal says node: command not found. What should you do first?
questions.explain: The installer adds Node.js to your PATH, the list of folders where the shell looks for programs. Old terminals still have the old list. If a new terminal also fails, restart the computer.
options: Install Node.js again from a different website
Close every terminal window and open a new one

questions.q: What is npm?
questions.explain: npm is installed together with Node.js. It installs packages, pieces of code other people published, such as ZudoJS.
options: A tool that comes with Node.js and installs packages other people published

questions.q: What does REPL stand for?
questions.explain: The REPL reads one line of JavaScript, evaluates (runs) it, prints the result, and loops back to wait for the next line.

questions.q: How do you start the Node.js REPL?
questions.explain: Typing node with nothing after it starts the REPL, and the prompt changes to >. node hello.js runs a file instead.

questions.q: In the REPL you type "Buy " + "milk". What does it show?
questions.explain: The result is text, and the REPL shows text in quotes so you can tell it apart from numbers. console.log would print it without quotes.

questions.q: In the REPL you type const tasks = ["Buy milk", "Write report"]. It shows undefined. What does that mean?
questions.explain: undefined means "no value". Storing something gives no result, but it worked: typing tasks.length next shows 2.
options: There is a mistake in the line
Storing a value produces no result; the list was stored under the name tasks

questions.q: In the REPL, console.log("Hi") shows Hi and then undefined. Why the undefined?
questions.explain: console.log does its job (printing) but returns no value. The REPL always shows the result of a line, so it shows undefined.
options: The text was not printed correctly
console.log printed the text, and itself gives back no value, which the REPL shows
The REPL prints every line twice
You must write console.log with a capital C in the REPL

questions.q: How do you leave the REPL?
questions.explain: .exit leaves the REPL. Ctrl + D, or Ctrl + C twice, does the same.

questions.q: Why do you write real programs in files instead of the REPL?
questions.explain: The REPL is great for a quick "what does this give?". But nothing is saved, so real programs go in files that you can run again and again.
options: Everything you type in the REPL is lost when you leave it
The REPL only runs one line per day
Files run faster than the REPL

questions.q: Your file is at src/app.js inside the current folder. How do you run it?
questions.explain: node needs the path of the file from the current folder. node app.js would look for app.js in the current folder and not find it.

questions.q: You changed hello.js. What do you do to see the new output?
questions.explain: Node.js runs the file as it is saved on disk at that moment. Save, then run the command again. Up brings back the last command.
options: Nothing: Node.js reruns it on its own
Save the file, then run node hello.js again (press Up to get it back)

questions.q: What does package.json record?
questions.explain: Every Node.js project has a package.json. npm init -y writes one for you with the project's name, version and other settings.
options: The project's name and the packages it uses
The history of every change to your files

questions.q: What does npm init -y do?
questions.explain: npm init creates package.json. -y ("yes") accepts all the default answers, so you are not asked any questions.
options: Creates a package.json for the current folder, accepting the default answers

questions.q: After npm init -y, the course runs npm pkg set type=module. Why?
questions.explain: npm init -y writes "type": "commonjs", the old way of splitting code into files. ES modules are the modern way. After the command, the line says "type": "module".
options: To switch the project from CommonJS to ES modules, the modern way that every ZudoJS package uses
To make the project run in the browser only

questions.q: You run npm pkg set type=module and it prints nothing. What happened?
questions.explain: Like many commands, it is silent on success. Open package.json to check: the last line now says "type": "module".
options: It failed; run it again with sudo
It worked; the command prints nothing on success

questions.q: What is a comment in JavaScript?
questions.explain: // starts a comment until the end of the line, and /* … */ wraps a comment over several lines. Node.js ignores both.
options: A line that prints text to the screen
A note for people, which Node.js skips completely
A statement that runs before all the others
An error message written by Node.js

questions.q: Which comment is the most useful?
questions.explain: Good comments explain why the code is written this way. "print the tasks" only repeats what the code already says.
options: // this is a line of code
// prices are in cents to avoid rounding errors

questions.q: A file is console.log("Hello from Node.js!); with the closing quote missing. What happens when you run it?
questions.explain: Without the closing ", the text never ends, which breaks JavaScript's grammar. Node.js rejects the whole file with SyntaxError: Invalid or unexpected token.
options: A SyntaxError: the file breaks the grammar, so nothing runs

questions.q: A file is Console.log("Hi");. What error do you get?
questions.explain: JavaScript is case-sensitive: Console is a different name from console, and no Console exists. The grammar is fine, so the file starts and fails at that line.
options: No error; capitals do not matter

questions.q: Which three things should you read in a Node.js error?
questions.explain: The top says where (file and line), the name says what kind (SyntaxError, ReferenceError, TypeError), and the message says what is wrong. The at node:internal… lines are inside Node.js, not your code.
options: The Node.js version, the date and the at node:internal lines
The file and line at the top, the error name, and the message

questions.q: A file has a missing " on line 1, Console.log on line 2 and a missing ) on line 3. Which error do you see first?
questions.explain: Syntax errors stop the whole file before anything runs, so Node.js reports one of them first. The capital C is only found while the code runs, after the grammar is fixed.
options: A SyntaxError; the ReferenceError only shows once the syntax errors are fixed
The ReferenceError on line 2, because it comes before line 3
No error: line 1 prints, then the program stops

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: In a file, console.log prints the text without quotes. The extra undefined only appears in the REPL or the devtools Console.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Everything after // is skipped. That includes the whole line with "Walk the dog": putting // in front of code is a common way to switch it off.
options:
My tasks for today:
- Buy milk
- Write report

My tasks for today:
- Buy milk
- Walk the dog
- Write report

This program prints a short task list.
My tasks for today:
- Buy milk
- Write report

My tasks for today:
- Buy milk // a comment can also end a line
- Write report

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Everything between /* and */ is one comment, even across several lines, so the two lines inside it never run.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: console.log prints all its values on one line, with one space between them. The commas in the code are not printed.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: * runs before -, so 10 * 3 - 4 is 30 - 4, which is 26.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Numbers without quotes are calculated: 7 days × 24 hours × 60 minutes is 10080. 1440 is only one day, and 168 is the hours in a week.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Text in quotes is printed exactly as written. Without quotes, 7 * 24 is a calculation, so it prints 168.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: const tasks = … stores the list under the name tasks. tasks.length is how many items it holds: 2.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: + joins texts exactly as they are. The first has a space at the end of "Buy ", the second does not. In a file, console.log shows no quotes.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Console with a capital C is a name that does not exist, so JavaScript throws a ReferenceError. The catch prints its name and message instead of crashing.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Statements run from top to bottom, one after another, and each console.log prints one line.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A comment can end a line after the code. Node.js runs the code before it and skips the comment.
questions.code:
console.log("Tasks:", 3); // 3 tasks today
console.log("Done:", 1); /* only one done */
options:
Tasks: 3 // 3 tasks today
Done: 1 /* only one done */

Tasks: 3 3 tasks today
Done: 1 only one done

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: consol is misspelt, but the grammar is still fine. The name simply does not exist, which is a ReferenceError when that line runs.

questions.q: Print three lines: My name is Ada, I want to build a task API, and Lessons in this course: 84. For the last line, give console.log the text and the number 84 as two values.
questions.explain: One console.log per line. In the last one, separate the text and the number with a comma: console.log("Lessons in this course:", 84).
questions.expected:
My name is Ada
I want to build a task API
Lessons in this course: 84

questions.q: Print how many minutes there are in a week (7 days of 24 hours of 60 minutes). Let JavaScript do the maths. The output must be Minutes in a week: 10080.
questions.explain: Write the calculation without quotes, 7 * 24 * 60, so JavaScript works it out. In quotes it would be printed as text.
questions.starter: // print the minutes in a week

questions.q: This program has three mistakes. Fix them so it prints Shopping list:, - Bread and - Milk, one per line.
questions.explain: Line 1 was missing a closing ", line 2 used Console with a capital C, and line 3 was missing a ).

questions.q: This program stops with ReferenceError: Console is not defined. Fix it so it prints Hello from Node.js!
questions.explain: JavaScript is case-sensitive. The name is console with a small c.

questions.q: The second task is switched off with a comment. Change the code so all three tasks print: - Buy milk, - Walk the dog, - Write report.
questions.explain: Remove the // at the start of the line. Node.js skips everything after //, so the line only runs once the comment marker is gone.
questions.expected:
- Buy milk
- Walk the dog
- Write report

questions.q: Use comments to switch off the two debug lines, without deleting them. The program should print only Start and End.
questions.explain: Put // in front of each debug line, or wrap both in /* … */. Node.js skips comments, so those lines no longer run.

questions.q: Finish the catch block so it prints the error's name, a colon, and its message. The program should print ReferenceError: Console is not defined.
questions.explain: Every error has a name and a message. error.name + ":" glues the colon to the name, and the comma adds a space before the message.

questions.q: Print two lines: the hours in a week and the seconds in a day. The output must be Hours in a week: 168 and then Seconds in a day: 86400.
questions.explain: Let JavaScript calculate: 7 * 24 and 24 * 60 * 60. Give console.log the text and the result as two values.
questions.starter: // print the hours in a week, then the seconds in a day
questions.expected:
Hours in a week: 168
Seconds in a day: 86400
questions.solution:
console.log("Hours in a week:", 7 * 24);
console.log("Seconds in a day:", 24 * 60 * 60);

questions.q: Print My tasks for today:, then each task on its own line starting with - , then Tasks: 2 Done: 0 using one console.log with four values.
questions.explain: Four statements print four lines. In the last one, console.log prints its four values on one line with spaces between them.
questions.expected:
My tasks for today:
- Buy milk
- Write report
Tasks: 2 Done: 0
